first_impression: The master key idea is clear and a bit alarming, which is probably the point. But I have heard this kind of pitch from every vendor this year, so I want to know who you are, who has bought this, and what it costs me before I give you more of my 20 minutes.
understood_riskmandate: partly: I get that it writes one page per agent showing what it can touch versus what it should touch, but I do not know if it is software, a consultancy service or a certificate, and I do not know who would stand behind a Licence to Operate.

steps.reaction: That is your homework, not mine, but it is nice that you came prepared; just do not tell me you read my company page and then get my business wrong.
'Does it have permission?' is a fair question and I honestly cannot answer it today, which is uncomfortable, so you have my attention.
The new employee with a master key is something I can repeat to my board, and that is useful, though it is a bit simple for a COO who runs 900 people.

You want me to list our agents and what they can reach, typed into your tool: who sees that data, where does it go, and I am not putting claims or customer system details into anything with test keys.
A red ring on my own situation is the part I would actually show my board, but I can see it is not built yet, and a picture of a risk is not proof of one.
One page my security team, my board and my insurer all read is attractive, but will my regulator and my insurer actually accept it, or is this just your document?
A link and a QR code is fine and low pressure; a copy that works offline is thoughtful, but today I only get a web page link, which is thin.
Good that a person reads the message before it is sent, since I do not want an AI emailing me, though I would like to know what you keep about me.
Writing a real policy for one real agent is a sensible small start, but 'no promises on price' means I cannot take it to anyone yet, and that is where a lot of vendors lose me.

moment_most_convinced: Step 5, the gap picture, because it turns something abstract into a red area I could show my board; step 2 is close behind because it names a question I cannot answer.
moment_lost_interest: Step 4, because I am asked to describe my agents and their access to a vendor I have just met, with only test keys, and no word on confidentiality or where the data goes. Step 9 also loses me because of no price or terms.
unanswered_questions: Who is RiskMandate, who has used it, and who stands behind the Licence to Operate if something goes wrong?
Will my regulator and my insurer accept this document, and has either ever seen one?
What happens to the information I type about our agents and systems, and who can see it?
How much of my team's time does a first policy take, and what will it cost me?
Does it check what the agent really does, or only what we tell you it does?
would_take_next_step: maybe: I would need a named reference from a regulated firm, a plain statement on data handling, a rough time and cost range for one pilot policy, and evidence that an insurer or regulator has read this kind of page.
plan_comments: The five steps read as a list of things you are building, not things I get, and the buyer parts (live infographic, animation, offline pack) are all still plans. The offline pack for a customer to share inside the company is the most useful bit for me, because I will have to sell this to my board. I would want evidence and pricing in the plan as much as pictures.
top_3_changes: Add a step early on who RiskMandate is and who vouches for it: a named customer or regulator or insurer reference, plus what a Licence to Operate is worth and who issues it.

Before step 4, say plainly how my information is handled, and offer a safe way in, such as a made-up example agent or a sample from my sector, instead of asking me to describe my real agents on the spot.
Give step 9 a real answer: a rough time and cost range for a first policy and a pilot, or at least how pricing works, so I can take something concrete to my board.
